implementation_notes: C has no generics, no virtual functions and no runtime type information, so the pattern is built by hand: the concrete value is addressed as void* (or stored as inline bytes plus a size) and the operations live in a const struct of function pointers - the manual vtable - together with destroy (and clone when values are copied) callbacks. The classic instances are the qsort comparator, which receives the elements erased as const void*, and GObject, where each instance points at a class struct holding the vtable and interfaces are structs of function pointers the implementor fills in. Where the type set is closed, a tagged union (struct { enum tag; union { ... } }) is the simpler and safer alternative; void* erasure is justified when the container must accept types it cannot enumerate.
pitfalls: void* erases qualifiers and type: recovering the value through the wrong type is undefined behaviour under strict aliasing, so every cast back must target exactly the stored type.
The vtable must carry destroy (and clone when copies are made) - without a destructor hook the erased value's resources leak, because the container cannot free what it cannot name.

Alignment and lifetime: storing the address of a stack temporary or casting between differently aligned objects corrupts memory; copy the value into storage the container owns or document the pointer's required lifetime.
